name: Guardian cryptic crossword, Penguin book 5 No 45

book.title: The New Penguin Book of The Guardian Crosswords, volume 5

entries.clue: Left show in relief (3,3)

blocks.note: the past tense of the departure: the walkers left at dawn
a dark mount shows a pale picture up by standing behind it

annotation.surface: An exhibition of relief carving, over on the left-hand side.
annotation.walkthrough: The second sense is the jeweller's and the framer's: a plain setting displays a stone by contrast with it. 'Left' is the past tense of a verb throughout, never the direction the surface offers.
annotation.definitionFit: To set off is to depart, and also to show a thing up by contrast, which is what putting it in relief does.

entries.clue: William endlessly promises to pay for livery (7)

indicatorNotes.endlessly: What is endless has no end, so the name in front of it gives up its final letter.

blocks.note: William shortens to Bill, and the deletion takes the last letter off it
an IOU is a scribbled promise to pay, and more than one of them adds the S

annotation.surface: William settles the bill for a servant's uniform with an unending stream of IOUs.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Livery' is the footman's uniform in the surface and an old adjective in the definition: livery means liverish, out of sorts. IOU is the crossword's standard promise to pay and turns up wherever a clue mentions debt.
annotation.definitionFit: Bilious means suffering from a disordered liver, which is what the adjective 'livery' says of a person — nothing to do with a uniform.

entries.clue: A score-draw also included everybody (3,3,3)

indicatorNotes.included: Something included has been taken inside what was there already, so the short word goes into the middle of the result.

blocks.note: a match finishing one goal each is a score draw, and the result is read aloud as one all
and = also, the word that tacks an extra item on

annotation.surface: A match that finished level, with everybody taken into account.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Score' wants to be twenty, the old word for it; here it is the football result, and a 1-1 draw is spoken rather than written. The smallest word in the clue supplies three of the nine letters.
annotation.definitionFit: One and all is the phrase for the whole company at once — 'welcome, one and all' takes in everybody present.

entries.clue: Take away forcibly and reportedly relax (5)

indicatorNotes.reportedly: What is reported is passed on by mouth, so the word behind it is wanted as a sound and not as a spelling.

blocks.note: to relax is to rest, and the silent letter in front makes no difference to the ear

annotation.surface: Snatching something away and then, by all accounts, putting your feet up.
annotation.walkthrough: The opening W is silent, so the two words are identical in the mouth and one letter apart on the page. The surface hides the join by making 'and' look like the second half of a thief's afternoon.
annotation.definitionFit: To wrest a thing is to twist it out of somebody's grip, taking it by force rather than by asking.

entries.clue: Having spikes, metal, fixed without difficulty (5)

indicatorNotes.without: To be without a thing is to be lacking it, so the letters of what the clue names next come out of the word they were in.

blocks.note: tin is the metal
fixed is HITCHED, a hitch is a difficulty, and HITCHED less those five letters leaves two

annotation.surface: A piece of metal fastened into place with no trouble at all.
annotation.walkthrough: The idiom under 'without difficulty' is 'without a hitch', and the word being stripped is never written down — the solver has to supply it from 'fixed'. A tine is the prong of a fork, a rake or a stag's antler.
annotation.definitionFit: A fork's tines are its prongs, so anything tined carries a row of spikes along it.

entries.clue: Motorist, a wag with a flower (3-6)

blocks.note: a card is a joker, the one who keeps the room laughing
a river flows, which makes it a thing that flows

annotation.surface: A driver with a taste for practical jokes, carrying a single bloom.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A flower' is the oldest trap in the British cryptic: not a bloom but something that flows, which is why a nine-letter answer needs no garden. The comma after the definition is all that separates it from the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A car-driver is a motorist — the person at the wheel, named for the vehicle rather than for the licence.

entries.clue: Member of family, aloof, American, in the money (7,6)

indicatorNotes.in: 'in' puts what stands before it inside what stands after, so the two letters land in the middle of the money.

blocks.note: a distant manner is an aloof one, keeping people at arm's length
money in the hand is coin, and the word opens after its second letter
US = American

annotation.surface: A stand-offish American relative who is not short of money.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In the money' is a phrase the surface uses whole, meaning well off, and the wordplay breaks it into an instruction plus a four-letter word. The answer runs on into 15 across.
annotation.definitionFit: A distant cousin is a relative several removes away, family on paper rather than in practice.

entries.clue: See 13
What a patrolling PC does in enclosures before the strike (6,3,4)

indicatorNotes.before: 'before' fixes the order of the two pieces: what it names comes second, so the enclosures are written down first.

blocks.note: a pound is the enclosure a stray dog or a towed car is shut in until claimed
a beat is a stroke or blow, the strike of a drummer's stick

annotation.surface: A police constable walking his rounds among the pens before the industrial action starts.
annotation.walkthrough: PC is the British police constable, the bobby on foot. 'The strike' asks for a blow rather than a picket line, and that is the sense the surface works hardest to hide. The answer runs on into 19 across.
annotation.definitionFit: To pound the beat is to walk a policeman's round on foot, tramping the same streets shift after shift.

entries.clue: See 17
Puzzler’s obscure ardour, by the sound of i it (9)

indicators: by the sound of i it

indicatorNotes.by the sound of i it: 'By the sound of it' asks for what the words in front sound like rather than how they are spelt; the stray letter is a slip in the book's type.

blocks.note: a misty morning is obscure, and said aloud the first five letters answer to it
ardour is fire in the belly, and the four letters that finish the answer sound exactly like it

annotation.surface: A crossword setter's hidden passion, murky and only to be guessed at.
annotation.walkthrough: Both halves have to be said aloud, and the join between them disappears in the mouth. The stray letter before 'it' is a slip in the book's type rather than any part of the clue.
annotation.definitionFit: A mystifier is one who mystifies, so it is a puzzler in the active sense — the setter, not the solver stuck on a clue.

entries.clue: Flags, perhaps, beginning to panic birds (5)

indicatorNotes.beginning to: The beginning of a word is the letter it starts with, and that single letter is all this takes from what follows.

blocks.note: the first letter of panic
Aves is the zoologist's class name for birds, the Latin plural of avis

annotation.surface: The first stirrings of panic send a flock of birds up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flags' is a verb here and the stones are flagstones — nothing to do with banners, and nothing to do with energy flagging either. Aves is the scientific class that covers every bird there is.
annotation.definitionFit: To flag a yard is to lay flagstones across it, one way of paving it — 'perhaps' marks flagging as an example rather than the whole word.

entries.clue: Railway fare’s about right (5)

indicatorNotes.about: What is about a thing is set round it, so the word in front opens up to take the letter that follows.

blocks.note: tack is an old word for food or provisions
r = right

annotation.surface: A rail ticket costing roughly the right amount.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Railway fare' reads as the price of a ticket, and the clue's split falls between those two words. Tack for food survives in Britain mainly in 'hard tack', the rock-hard biscuit sailors were issued at sea.
annotation.definitionFit: The track is the permanent way a train runs on, so it stands for the railway itself rather than for the service that uses it.

entries.clue: Not straying from stronghold, GI not troubled (7,2)

indicatorNotes.troubled: Troubled water will not lie still, and letters described that way are to be stirred into some other order.

blocks.note: the keep is the strongest tower of a castle, the last place to fall
the soldier and the little word after him, five letters in a new order

annotation.surface: An American soldier untroubled by being shut up in a fortress.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Not' looks as though it cancels the instruction beside it and is in fact part of what gets stirred. GI is the American private, named for the 'government issue' stamped on his kit.
annotation.definitionFit: To keep to a path is not to stray from it, and the phrase does the same job for rules, promises and timetables.

entries.clue: Dairy product giving small child an awful dread (7)

indicatorNotes.an awful: An awful anything is in a bad way, and letters in a bad way do not keep the order they came in.

blocks.note: ch is the standard short form of child, as printed on fare tables
the five letters of dread in a new arrangement

annotation.surface: A dairy product that leaves a small child horribly frightened.
annotation.walkthrough: Cheese before bed is supposed to bring bad dreams, which is why the surface holds together so smoothly. 'Small' is not describing the child at all — it asks for the short form of the word.
annotation.definitionFit: Cheddar is the cheese named after the Somerset village, and cheese is made from milk, so the definition names the family the wordplay pins down.

entries.clue: Stick the woman in a private retreat without limit (6)

indicatorNotes.in: 'in' names the place a thing goes into, so the woman is set inside the letters that follow.
indicatorNotes.without limit: A limit is the edge a thing stops at, and a word without it loses the letter at its end.

blocks.note: a den is somebody's private retreat, with the clue's own A in front of it
her is the woman, in the crossword's usual shorthand

annotation.surface: Shutting a woman away in a private hideaway for an unlimited stay.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Without limit' reads as 'indefinitely' in the surface and is a deletion in the wordplay — the limit of a word being the letter it ends on. 'Stick' is the verb glue does, not the shoving the sentence suggests.
annotation.definitionFit: To adhere is to stick — what glue does to paper, and what a loyal member does to a cause.

entries.clue: Rushed around abroad and sermonised (7)

indicatorNotes.around: What goes around a thing closes on it from both sides, so the letters in front part to let the next piece in.

blocks.note: a car that sped was rushing
somebody abroad is out of the country

annotation.surface: A traveller dashing about overseas and preaching at everybody he meets.
annotation.walkthrough: To spout is to hold forth at length and to little purpose, which is the dismissive word for it. 'Around' belongs to the rushing in the surface and is the instruction that prises the first piece apart.
annotation.definitionFit: To spout is to talk on and on in a self-important way, which is what 'sermonised' says about a speaker who will not stop.

entries.clue: To attach the thing standing upside down takes an age (3,2)

indicatorNotes.standing upside down: Something upside down is read from its far end, and in a down entry that means the bottom letter comes first.

blocks.note: the thing is IT, turned end for end
an eon is an immense stretch of time

annotation.surface: Fastening the object the wrong way up is taking for ever.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Takes an age' is the exasperated idiom of the surface and three plain letters underneath. In a down clue 'upside down' is meant literally: the word is read from the foot of the column upwards.
annotation.definitionFit: To tie something on is to attach it, the way a label is tied on to a parcel by its string.

entries.clue: Dandy depicted on paper, with the join not visible? (4-5)

blocks.note: dandy in the sense of splendid, as in 'fine and dandy'
what a pencil does to paper

annotation.surface: A portrait of a dandy on paper, with no seam anywhere in it.
annotation.walkthrough: Fine-drawing is the darner's craft: a tear sewn up so closely that the repair cannot be found afterwards. The question mark owns the fact that the definition describes the answer rather than translating it.
annotation.definitionFit: Cloth that is fine-drawn has been mended so finely that the mend cannot be seen, which is exactly a join left invisible.

entries.clue: Warrior’s belt, unadorned and less than sumptuous (7)

indicatorNotes.less than: 'Less than' is short of the whole, so the word it heads is taken one letter short of its end.

blocks.note: a bald statement is unadorned, with nothing added to soften it
sumptuous is RICH, and this stops one letter before the end of it

annotation.surface: A plain sword-belt that turns out not to be as splendid as it looked.
annotation.walkthrough: A baldric is the belt slung over one shoulder and across the chest to carry a sword or a bugle. 'Less than sumptuous' reads as faint praise and is an instruction to stop early.
annotation.definitionFit: A baldric is the shoulder belt a fighting man wears to carry his sword, so it belongs to a warrior by trade.

entries.clue: To speak more softly will get inferior person’s approval (5,4,5)

blocks.note: the lower orders are the inferior ones, below the rest in rank
one is the formal word for a person, and the apostrophe-s rides along with it
a voice is a vote or an expressed opinion — a committee that speaks with one voice

annotation.surface: Speaking more quietly earns you the approval of your social inferior.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Inferior person's approval' reads as a single phrase and comes apart into three separate pieces, which is where the difficulty sits. The answer runs on into 6 down.
annotation.definitionFit: To lower one's voice is to drop from an ordinary tone to a quiet one, which is speaking more softly.

entries.clue: See 5
Roman god brooded, standing on vessel (6)

indicatorNotes.standing on: One thing standing on another is above it, and in a down entry what is above is written first.

blocks.note: a hen broods by sitting on her eggs
an urn is a vessel, the crossword's favourite one

annotation.surface: A Roman god sulking on top of a jar.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Brooded' is the hen's sense rather than the sulker's, which is how three letters come out of a word about mood. Saturn was the god of sowing and harvest, and Saturday is named after him.
annotation.definitionFit: Saturn is the Roman god of seed and harvest, father of Jupiter, whose midwinter festival gave us the word saturnalia.

entries.clue: Scholar’s crib may bring success (6)

blocks.note: an MA is a Master of Arts, a scholar by degree
the apostrophe-s is read as a plain S
a crib and a cot are the same bed for a baby

annotation.surface: A student's smuggled cheat-sheet that might just see him through.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Crib' is the schoolboy's cheat-sheet in the surface and the baby's bed in the wordplay, and the same word doing both jobs is the whole clue. Nothing admits that the scholar is a degree rather than a person.
annotation.definitionFit: A mascot is the charm or creature a team keeps for luck, so it is precisely a thing that may bring success.

entries.clue: Swan copes remarkably in winter scene (9)

indicatorNotes.remarkably: What is remarkable is out of the ordinary, and letters put out of their ordinary arrangement come back in a new one.

blocks.note: nine letters for the pile

annotation.surface: A swan managing surprisingly well in the depths of winter.
annotation.walkthrough: The picture is so plausible — a bird on a frozen lake — that the first two words read as a subject and its verb instead of as nine letters waiting to be rearranged.
annotation.definitionFit: A snowscape is a stretch of country lying under snow, the winter counterpart of a landscape.

entries.clue: Pitmen due to be abandoned, like neglected dustbins? (9)

indicatorNotes.abandoned: Abandoned behaviour is wild and unrestrained, and letters in that state will not hold the order they were given.

blocks.note: nine letters for the pile

annotation.surface: Miners about to be left to their fate, treated like bins nobody has collected.
annotation.walkthrough: The comparison carries the clue: men thrown aside like rubbish left at the kerb. Pitmen are coal miners, named for the pit they went down, and 'abandoned' looks like their fate rather than an instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: A bin nobody has come for is unemptied, still holding everything that was put into it last week.

entries.clue: Waterproof for sophisticated New Yorker? (7)

blocks.note: the long oilskin raincoat, which is what Americans call it
the smooth, worldly townsman who knows his way about, set against his country cousin

annotation.surface: A raincoat picked out for a smart city type.
annotation.walkthrough: Both halves are American, which is why New York is named: the coat and the smooth operator are one word on that side of the Atlantic. The question mark admits that any big city would have served.
annotation.definitionFit: A slicker is the American oilskin raincoat, and a city slicker is a smooth, worldly townsman — the sophisticate the second half points at.

entries.clue: Faced holy man, single, petrified (6,2,5)

blocks.note: to face somebody is to turn to them
st is the short form of saint
single = one

annotation.surface: Coming face to face with an unmarried holy man and freezing in terror.
annotation.walkthrough: Petrify is Latin for making into stone, so the definition and the answer are one idea in two languages. 'Faced' has to give up two words at once, which is the step that stays hidden longest. The answer runs on into 20 down.
annotation.definitionFit: Petrified means turned to stone, from the Latin petra, a rock — and English uses the same word for somebody rigid with fright.

entries.clue: See 19
Rotten time in City area makes one throw up (6)

indicatorNotes.Rotten: Something rotten has fallen apart, and letters that have fallen apart are put back in a different arrangement.
indicatorNotes.in: 'in' names the place a thing goes into, so the letters before it are set inside the word that follows.

blocks.note: EC is the postal district covering the City of London, the square mile of banks and insurers
the four letters of time in another order

annotation.surface: A bad spell in the financial district leaves you feeling sick.
annotation.walkthrough: The City with a capital C is London's banking quarter, and every postcode in it begins EC. 'Makes one throw up' is the definition, though it reads like one more complaint about the job.
annotation.definitionFit: An emetic is a medicine given to bring on vomiting, so it is exactly a thing that makes one throw up.

entries.clue: Connected, capitally trimmed, and daubed with dark liquid (5)

indicatorNotes.capitally trimmed: The capital of a word is the letter at its head, and trimming a thing cuts that head off.

blocks.note: two things connected are linked
this L stands at the head of LINKED and is the letter trimmed away

annotation.surface: Something joined up, neatly cut back, and smeared with something dark.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Capitally' is the old adverb for splendidly, which is how the surface takes it; the wordplay wants the capital as the head of a thing. Both readings lean on 'trimmed' meaning tidily cut as well as shortened.
annotation.definitionFit: Something inked has had ink daubed over it, the dark liquid being named by what it does rather than by what it writes.

entries.clue: It’s not specific against a shivering fit (5)

blocks.note: v is short for versus, the against of a fixture list
an ague is a fever whose symptom is violent shivering

annotation.surface: Somebody being unhelpfully unspecific about a bout of the shivers.
annotation.walkthrough: The v of a football fixture — Arsenal v Spurs — is the whole story of the first letter. Ague is the old name for malarial fever, kept alive by Shakespeare and by crosswords.
annotation.definitionFit: Something vague is not specific: it leaves the details blurred instead of naming them.
